entry.title: Raymond Zeitler: Emacs Windows Management With windmove
entry.summary:
0
Recently I came across the windmove functions1. This discovery caused me to lose interest in bookmarks; now bookmarks are a mere curiosity.
The windmove functions allow you to "operate" on a window; the target window is given as a direction relative to point. Operations include:
selection, like next-window, but direction overrides window order deletion, like delete-window, but direction indicates the window to delete buffer display (not yet in use by the author) S-<left>, S-<right>, S-<up>, S-<down> for window selection. For example, you can activate the window on the left with windmove-left or S-<left>.
Org users already press S-<left> (and S-<right>) on a heading to change TODO status. As well, we press S-<up> (and S-<down>) to increase (decrease) a heading's priority. Luckily, it's easy to specify a different modifier key. I configured my system to make windmove-dir respond to M-s-<dir>2 with the following statement:
(windmove-default-keybindings '(meta super))
windmove-delete-left. I've defined C-M-s-<dir>3 for the windmove-delete-dir functions by adding this to my init file:
(windmove-delete-default-keybindings '(control meta super))
other-window (C-x o), sometimes "overshooting" the desired window, or I'd resort to using the mouse to click in it. Now with this intuitive method of selecting windows, I can keep my hands on the keyboard and spend less time figuring out how to get around.
Try it out!
0 See: https://ray-on-emacs.blogspot.com/2026/11/emacs-carnival-november-2026.html
1 Emacs windmove help page
2 On Windows, I hold down the Alt and Win keys while pressing an arrow key.
3 As above, but additionally with the Control key. It's surprisingly easy, in fact.

entry.title: Irreal: Manual Dired Search
entry.summary:
The Art Of Not Asking Why reminds us of a very useful technique for iteratively searching through a series of files for those that contain a given set of terms. The process if simple but very flexible:
Open a Dired buffer with the files you want to search. Use %g to do a regular expression search through the files for one of the terms. The files containing the term will be marked. Use t to toggle the marks, resulting in all the files that don’t contain the term being marked. Use k to temporarily hide the marked files, leaving only those that contain the term. Go to step 2 using the next term. A command to search through the contents of the marked files and show the results in another buffer.
The nice thing about this method is that it’s interactive: you progressively narrow down the list of target files by eliminating files that don’t contain the terms your looking for. You can, as JTR says, even manually eliminate files that you don’t want to consider as you go along. It’s a good technique and worth remembering.

entry.title: Blackpool To Coach: Happy Birthday, You’re Fired
entry.summary: Much derision fell upon the people who run Blackpool Football Club of League One, the third tier of English football, when it wished head coach Ian Evatt a happy birthday seven hours before firing him on Thursday. It did seem exceedingly cruel, even by the prevailing bastardy standards of our time. Then again, only a simp would believe that human decency enters into decisions like these. Your holidays aren't anyone else's, so stop acting like they are. This is especially true when the only thing keeping you out of a relegation spot is goal differential. In that situation, your employer very well might call you "Gaffer" in the morning and can you by happy hour. That's the gig. The rudimentarily funny part is how the club announced his firing. According to them, Evatt "departed his role," as though he chose to fire himself. This is not just an English politeness thing, either. Teams and the media types who exist to disseminate their team sources' text messages love to describe firings as "a parting of ways," or the coach "leaving his role," or beating feet "by mutual agreement," and over time, that creeps into the language used by normal fans. It's as if we each have an HR goblin in our homes, ready to spring malevolently into action at any moment.

entry.title: ‘Madden’ Makes One Of The NFL’s Biggest Characters Feel Silly And Small
entry.summary: Al Davis's afterlife is difficult enough to imagine under any circumstances, but it takes an exceptionally grisly imagination to make him a character in a Hallmark movie written in an hour by a seventh grader. And to add imaginary insult to conceptual injury, Davis has been made into a supporting character in a Hallmark movie written in an hour by a seventh grader. The actual film is not made by Hallmark, where superficiality is raised to raison d'etre and plotting and dialogue are upstaged by tinsel and presents strewn about the town gazebo, but by Amazon. Less explicably, it is co-written and directed by David O. Russell, and not a middle schooler on a deadline. It is called Madden and is about John Madden, mostly, and most of what Christian Bale does as Al Davis amounts to reacting to things that Nicolas Cage, as John Madden, does. It's a romcom without the rom and precious little com. Now that's making hell relatable to us all. As you may have already heard, Madden is galactically bad. It's a movie about a man far too large for the biopic genre, maybe even two such men if you want to raise Davis to Madden's cultural stature, and that's its essential problem. There is a lot of competition, there, but "fundamentally should not exist" is hard to top as problems go. It's also a movie released around the holidays, when movie IQs are lowered by a good 25 points by the mere act of their being released to a national audience preparing for its own annual festive stupefaction.

entry.title: Victor Wembanyama’s Blister Inspires Purely Downward Jump Shot
entry.summary:
The thrown-in dunk, or "thrunk" if you prefer, is no new phenomenon. Vertically gifted players have long been hurling basketballs down into the hoop from a distance, without their hands directly touching the rim. But has that hurling motion ever been replaced by the soft wrist flick of a jump shot? Have you seen a jump shot begin from above the rim? On Thursday night, San Antonio Spurs center Victor Wembanyama developed his own variation on the thrunk, after collecting a hit-ahead pass from his teammate Stephon Castle. All alone on the other end, Wemby went up with a guide hand on the side of the ball, and with his shooting hand he flicked the ball directly down into the hoop. In the official play-by-play, it was logged as a pedestrian "running dunk," but the truth is out there. We saw the shunk.

entry.title: It’s Familiar At The Top
entry.summary: Welcome to the Defector College Football Watch Guide, where Israel Daramola and Ray Ratto will tell you which of the weekend’s college football games are worth giving a crap about. Ray: Last week went a long way toward revealing December and January, which sucks a bit because most of the surviving mysteries regarding conference championships, playoff berths and firings are largely being settled. The weekend highlights included Oklahoma pitching hissy fits at Ole Miss and the SEC office over uncontrollable travel issues, then winning on Sunday; Arizona State reinventing pregame prep by flying to Orlando on game day to beat UCF, 26-13; and Washington State getting its second win of the season by beating Colorado State, 73-7, with nine rushing touchdowns. Most of the remaining slate was watching the form of the last two months solidify and harden into an easily predictable future. For all the chaos we yammer about, the same old stories are being told the same old way because college football is devoted to business as usual, plus the hiring hall at James Madison. There isn't even the manufactured drama of whether Notre Dame will get in the College Football Playoff (it will), or whether USC will (it won't). The first hints of traditional rivalry games begin this weekend, but most of them will happen right after Thanksgiving, and the matchups we do get are circumstantially tepid. Frankly, if we were you (and believe us, nobody wants that in either direction), we'd sit out this week and wait for the last conference championships to be sorted. You won't miss much. Even the possibility of UMass (remember them?) nailing down its first bowl game since joining big-kid football is effectively over, after a 34-33 loss to lowly Akron on Wednesday. That makes us all feel like right charlies for getting our hopes up to begin with.

entry.title: Alex Ovechkin Is A Tough Watch These Days
entry.summary: It is becoming physically painful to watch Alexander Ovechkin play hockey. In this, his 22nd and final NHL season, all at once he has started to look his age. He hasn't been the most ... let's say ambulatory skater for years now, but he had somehow found ways to defy the calendar and continue to put up 30- and 40-goal seasons. That magic has run out. With just one goal in 20 games this season, none in his last 15, the NHL's greatest scorer is in the longest goal drought of his career. Over the last few years, Ovechkin's game has contracted to encompass only his shot. That snipe from the circle hadn't abandoned him, even as his footspeed did—he's the slowest forward in the league by both average and top skating speed. As long as he was scoring, it was easier to ignore, if still a little upsetting for anyone who remembers the freight train he was in his youth. But the shot's gone too, at least over the first quarter of the season. "Chances are there,” Ovechkin insisted Thursday night, after Washington's 6-3 home loss to Buffalo. “Sometimes you hold stick too tight." Without the goals, what's left is a large old man, skating stiffly and slowly up and down the neutral zone, waiting for his teammates to make something happen, because he can't backcheck, and he can't go coast to coast anymore. Against the Sabres, with the game already well out of hand, he was chased down from behind on a potential 2-on-1. An unmistakable sign it's time to hit the exits.

entry.title: “Mind If I Join?”
entry.summary: The winsome fly Istocheta aldrichi does not appear very winsome, unless you are also a fly. The fly looks like any other of its kind, with eyes as red as goji berries and a coat of horrible hairs. It is about the size of a housefly, and you probably would not be able to distinguish it from its more common counterpart if you saw one buzzing around your kitchen. Fortunately for you, however, the winsome fly has no interest in you and your humble human existence. The winsome fly is a parasitoid, and it only has big red eyes for the Japanese beetle, Popillia japonica. The Japanese beetle is the winsome fly's only known host, which explains in part why the fly above is staring so intently at the beetles. But the winsome fly has a trick up its hairy little sleeve. It has learned that the easiest way to parasitize the poor beetle is when the bug is at its most vulnerable, meaning when she is doing it—a beetle caught in the throes of beetle passion, an insect in flagrante delicto—per a new paper recently published in Biology Letters. "Don't mind if I do!"

entry.title: Irreal: Opening Techinfo Sourced Web Pages In Emacs
entry.summary:
interesting little utility. Although it’s restricted to Safari and the Mac, it’s a nice idea that could probably be ported to other operating systems without difficulty. The idea is to be able to easily move from reading a Web page generated by Techinfo to reading the same information with the Emacs Info reader.
Reading Info pages with Emacs is straightforward and comfortable but the external utilities to read them outside of Emacs are terrible. Therefore, a lot us who started with another editor learned to go to the Web first rather than try to navigate the horrible external reader packages. But, as Choi points out, recent events have shown us that we can’t always count on the Web being there for us.
Choi’s solution to all this is the Counterpart utility that provides a menu in Safari to open the Web page’s content in Emacs. Of course, this only works for Techinfo generated content. Your immediate reaction may be, “Who cares?” but I’ve sometimes wished for something like this so that I could have the content side by side with whatever I was working on in Emacs. That also make’s it easy to copy text out of the Info buffer when you want to add a quote to whatever you’re writing.

entry.title: Lars Ingebrigtsen: Herp derp I eat paste
entry.summary:
A year and a half ago I made a kitchen clock, which has worked well (except that I had to swap out the screen which broke mysteriously). But yesterday I was having some work done here, so I had to remove one of the wifi access points here, and… the clock stopped working. *gasp* Yes, because I had in my infinite wisdom decided that I would generate the clock face on a different machine, because the clock is a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, and I just assumed that it didn’t have enough memory to run Emacs (which I am, being a totally rational person, using to generate the SVG that’s being displayed). So it’s a Rube Goldberguesque setup of having the image being generated on the main server, and then scp‘d over once a minute, and then being displayed on the console here in the kitchen. But the wifi outage made me wonder — is it true that the machine doesn’t have enough memory to do it all on device?
So it’s got 416MB of useful memory, and while just running and doing nothing special, it’s using 129MB of that. What happens if I load an Emacs with all the SVG libraries and stuff and generate the image?
It’s using 186MB — so the Emacs occupies about 50MB max. *sigh* It’s so easy to think of Emacs as this “big thing”, but everything has gotten so much bigger around it that it doesn’t matter at all any more. So now I’ve changed the code to run on-device, so the only thing that goes AWOL if the wifi goes missing is updated temperatures.

entry.title: Charles Choi: Opening Texinfo Web Pages in Emacs Info
entry.summary: As convenient as accessing online services can be, any disruption in availability without a fallback is painful. Given events of late, many are learning the hard way what it’s like to live without that fallback. GNU Emacs has long supported reading documentation via the Info reader package. Info reader is a “local first” system, where all documentation is stored locally. The source format of the documentation is Texinfo which is exported to different formats, among them Info (used by the Emacs Info reader), HTML, and PDF. Texinfo exported HTML is typically hosted on a website (usually GNU Project), with each Info node mapped to a URL path and indexed by most major search engine services. Discovery of information in Texinfo documentation is frequently done via web search. If the user desires to view that Texinfo web page in the Emacs Info reader, that has to be done manually by corresponding the web page to its Info node. Counterpart is a new utility to automate opening the Info node counterpart of a Texinfo exported web page in Emacs. This utility is designed for Emacs users on macOS who also use the Safari web browser. It requires the installation of a macOS Shortcut which is run from the main menu bar. More detail on using it can be found in the Counterpart User Guide. Once a desired Info node is opened in Emacs, you can then bookmark it for later access, no internet connection required.

entry.title: Irreal: Setting The Timezone In Emacs
entry.summary:
hint for those of you who travel and phone home with Emacs. Here’s the situation: you are travelling and log into your home server with SSH and emacsclient. It’s wonderful. Just like being at home except the date/time stamp is wrong. The time and date are whatever your home server thinks they are but you want them to be local time.
The answer is simple. You simply need to change the TZ (timezone) environment variable to reflect your current location. For example, if you’ve travelled to New York (in the US) you would set TZ to “America/New_York”. Emacs, of course, provides a command to do this: (setenv "TZ" "America/New_York").
The zone codes can be a bit opaque so Choi has added a command to the latest Casual suite to set the TZ variable complete with completion. Take a look at his post if you’re interested.

We ask speakers to say their names at the beginning of their presentation, but people don't often include their last names, so the intro gets that consistently. …

entry.title: Charles Choi: Setting the Timezone in Emacs
entry.summary:
Here’s the problem: You are traveling in a different time zone from the Emacs server instance you are accessing remotely via ssh + emacsclient. All clock calculations in that Emacs session are using the local timezone relative to where the server is located. But what you really want is emacsclient to use the current timezone you are in, so things like the mode line clock render accordingly. To adjust the timezone in an Emacs session, use the command setenv to set the environment variable TZ with a timezone defined in the zoneinfo database. This can be called from Elisp as shown below.
1
(setenv "TZ" "Asia/Seoul")
The latest v3.1.0 update of Casual adds the command casual-timezone-set-tz that provides a completion interface for selecting a timezone to pass to setenv.
1
M-x casual-timezone-set-tz RET
Note that setting TZ impacts the Emacs session globally; any other running behavior depending on a clock should be taken into account.

entry.title: Irreal: Let Over Lambda Is Free To Read
entry.summary:
making his excellent book Let over Lambda available on line and as a PDF. I’ve written about the book several times most importantly here and here but you can search Irreal for “let over lambda” for the the others.
I can’t overemphasize the effect this book had on me. I learned a lot about Lisp and even programming from it. Some people complained that they didn’t like his approach to structuring his Lisp but I never had a problem with it.
The book is about Lisp Macros and the tremendous powers they provide. As an example, Hoyte gives a macro implementation of the Scheme named let construct. There are a lot more things like that in the book.
Let Over Lambda is about Common Lisp but a large portion of it applies to Elisp too. If you’d like to become really good at Elisp, Let Over Lambda is a good resource. As I said, it’s mostly about Common Lisp but a surprising amount carries over to Elisp.
In any event, you can check out the book for free and if you like what you see, you can read the entire book. It is, believe me, well worth your while.
